revisions.title: The danger of equal measures
revisions.body: The opening places the statesman's inquiry inside a promise: Theodorus says gratitude will become triple after the statesman and philosopher are worked out, and Socrates immediately rebukes his equal valuation of the three figures. The dramatic work is a hierarchy question, not a settled ranking; the passage makes the inquiry begin under that pressure.

revisions.title: Two measures, one practical test
revisions.body: One way to hear this passage is as a correction to two easy habits of judgment. “Greater” and “less” are first compared with one another; excess and deficiency are then considered against a mean—the fitting point for the matter at hand. The payoff, as I read it, is methodological: a discourse is not good because it is long or short, but because its divisions help the listener inquire more clearly. The mean is a test of fit, not an exact numerical standard.

Socrates’ rebuke turns Theodorus’ arithmetic into a measure of honor: the three figures have been assigned equal worth even though Socrates says their honor exceeds that proportion. The exchange does not ask us to settle the ranking; it makes equal valuation itself the object of playful correction.

At 258e, the Stranger divides sciences into practical and purely cognitive kinds, and Young Socrates accepts the division. This is the inquiry’s first cut; it does not yet say which side contains the statesman’s art.
